readingInstruction: Read Psalm 131, Psalm 133, and Psalm 134. These are three of the shortest psalms in the Psalter, and they are full. Read each one slowly. They teach childlike trust, brotherly unity, and a blessing at night.
settingTheScene: Three more Songs of Ascents. Psalm 131 is a psalm of David about quieting the soul. Psalm 133 celebrates the unity of God’s people. Psalm 134 is the last of the group of pilgrim songs before the final two, a call to the servants of the LORD who stand by night in the house of the LORD. Together they are a tender picture of what the pilgrim learned on the journey to Zion: humility, fellowship, and worship.
observation: “O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me” (131:1).
“But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me” (131:2).
“O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore” (131:3).
“Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!” (133:1).
“It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron” (133:2).
“It is like the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion!” (133:3).
“For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore” (133:3).
“Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD!” (134:1).
interpretation:
Psalm 131 is a prayer of humility and rest. David says, “My heart is not lifted up.” He is not proud and does not chase after impossible things. Then he describes how he has calmed his soul like a weaned child with its mother. A weaned child no longer fusses for milk but rests content in the mother’s arms, not because of what she provides, but because of who she is. This is a mature form of trust. It does not demand answers or benefits. It rests in the presence of the one who loves. The psalm ends with a call to Israel: hope in the LORD. Humility and hope go together.

Psalm 133 is a short celebration of unity. “Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!” The image is of two kinds of abundance. The first is the anointing oil poured on Aaron’s head, running down to his beard and the collar of his robes, a picture of a lavish, fragrant blessing that covers the whole person. The second is the dew of Hermon falling on Zion. It is refreshing and life-giving. The meaning is that unity among the people of God is not something small but a rich gift from God. And “there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore.” God commands blessing where his people dwell together.

Psalm 134 is the last of the set before the closing pair. It is a call to worship, spoken to the temple servants who keep watch by night. “Come, bless the LORD.” Their work is praise. They lift up their hands in the sanctuary and bless the LORD. Then the response comes: “May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!” The blessing goes both ways.

The whole sequence of pilgrim songs ends with a night watch and a blessing. After a long journey, the people arrive, and the end of the journey is worship.
connection: Jesus said, “Unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3). Matthew 11:28-29 invites those who are weary to take his yoke, for he is gentle and lowly in heart. John 17:20-23 shows Jesus praying that his people may be one. Ephesians 4:1-6 urges the unity of the Spirit. Colossians 3:14 says love binds everything together in perfect harmony. Revelation 7:15 shows the multitudes serving God day and night in his temple.
application:
Quiet your soul today. Sit for five minutes, like a weaned child with its mother, asking for nothing.

Work for unity in your church or family. Is there someone you need to forgive or reconcile with?

Pray Psalm 134 at the end of the day, as a night watch, blessing the LORD.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to quiet your soul like a weaned child.
Thank him for the gift of unity among his people.
Bless the LORD in your own words.
